lessons.title: Function definitions and calls
lessons.prepare: Python editor, the functions chapter and the familiar badge-cost calculation.

slides.title: Function definitions and calls
slides.notes: Success means identify a definition, make a call and trace a returned result. Link to earlier badge programs so learners focus on function structure rather than a new calculation.
body: Unit 1 · Week 5 · Lesson 1
Give a useful calculation a name and call it when needed.

slides.title: Retrieval: a familiar calculation
slides.notes: Allow one minute without notes, then compare. Four badges at $3 cost $12. Quantity and price are inputs to the calculation; multiplication produces the result. Distinguish calculation from input prompts and printing. Revisit arithmetic if needed before introducing syntax.
body: Four badges cost $3 each. What is the total?
Which values does the calculation need?
Which step calculates, and which step displays?
Compare your explanation with a partner.

slides.title: A function’s agreed task
slides.notes: Explain contract as agreed inputs, result and assumptions. Use non-negative whole-number quantities and whole-dollar prices in these introductory examples. The function returns quantity × unit_price. It does not prompt or print. The caller decides where values come from and how to use the result.

slides.title: A definition waits for a call
slides.notes: def creates the function, but its body runs when badge_cost(4,3) is called. Parameters receive 4 and 3, return sends 12 back, cost receives 12 and print displays it. Mark the indented body and unindented caller. Ask why a file containing only this definition prints nothing.
body: Predict what prints and when the body runs.
Identify the definition and the call.
slides.code:
def badge_cost(quantity, unit_price):
    return quantity * unit_price

cost = badge_cost(4, 3)
print(cost)

slides.title: A trace across the call
slides.notes: Model 4,3 as arguments, local parameter bindings and returned 12 stored in cost. Learners independently trace badge_cost(6,3): result 18. Support: provide stage headings. Stretch: trace badge_cost(0,3) and explain why it needs no special branch.

slides.title: Several calls, one definition
slides.notes: Keep one definition and make separate calls (0,3), (4,3), (4,5). Expected 0,12,20. Driver runs, navigator checks prior predictions and explains a call, then swap. Each learner records results. Support: supply one example call. Stretch: use a returned result in a later addition without changing the function.
body: Keep one badge_cost definition.
Predict calls with (0, 3), (4, 3) and (4, 5).
Run each call and record the returned result.
Swap roles and explain how the same body serves each call.

slides.title: Which line calls the function?
slides.notes: Correct B invokes the function. A defines it and C refers to the function object without calling it. Take simultaneous choices. If several choose A, run a file containing only the definition and ask what triggers its body.
body: A: def badge_cost(quantity, unit_price):
B: badge_cost(4, 3)
C: badge_cost
Choose the call and explain what triggers execution.

slides.title: Exit ticket: define, call and predict
slides.notes: badge_cost(5,2) returns 10, stored with cost = badge_cost(5,2). Definition creates the function; a call invokes it. Collect individual calls and explanations. Use errors to group definition-versus-call support next lesson.
body: Write a call for five badges at $2 each.
Predict the returned result.
Show how the caller could store that result.
Explain how a definition differs from a call.

lessons.title: Use parameters and returns to separate game rules
lessons.prepare: Before class verify the nominated editor uses a school-approved Python/Pygame installation. Extract the whole pygame-teaching-pack.zip into a writable disposable folder. Open https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-2 and workbook.md, faded_practice.py, practice-tests.csv and readiness.csv. Run python lab_runner.py 2. Use supplied named state/runner infrastructure; no student-authored classes, paid media or assessed project code. Record device, interpreter and support. Paper traces support reasoning; live window/keyboard evidence remains necessary. The suggested 55-minute allocation is untrialled; use the supplied 50-minute adaptation when required.

slides.title: Functions separate the game rules
body: Unit 1 · Week 5 · Lesson 2
Trace parameters, returns and deliberate state changes.
slides.notes: Run python lab_runner.py 2. This stage has movement and an active timer, with no station scoring. Success: explain new_state, command and update, restore reset values and show that a paused update changes neither x nor remaining time. Read state["mode"] as a supplied named slot. Dictionary infrastructure is provided; authoring dictionaries/classes is not a new Year 11 assessment requirement. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-2; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .

slides.title: Retrieve a call and its result
body: Which names are parameters in def area(w, h)?
Which values are arguments in area(7, 2)?
How do print and return differ?
slides.notes: Give silent thinking time. w and h are parameters; 7 and 2 are arguments; return w*h gives 14 to the caller. print displays text and a function without an explicit return value returns None on normal completion. Use one brief foundation trace, then transfer to the supplied lab functions. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-2; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .

slides.title: One function returns a fresh state
body: Each call creates a separate active list.
Trace values returning to the caller.
slides.notes: Excerpt from lab_rules.new_state. Run the supplied stage before tracing. The caller receives a state store; field meanings are mode, horizontal position, active milliseconds, score, active station flags and whether a result was saved. Values are supplied infrastructure. Calling new_state twice creates separate dictionaries/lists. Show that changing a local scalar name does not rebind the caller variable, whereas updating a shared state slot is deliberately visible to the caller. Keep the distinction concrete rather than adding dictionary theory. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-2; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .

slides.title: Trace the start, pause and reset rules
slides.notes: Run stage 2 using Space to start/pause/resume and R to reset. command(state, action) receives a supplied mutable state and deliberately changes it; its normal return value is None. The runner processes transitions before update and discards the delta on a start/resume/reset frame, so paused wall time is not charged on resuming. Reset restores x=308, 20000 ms, score 0, fresh active flags and saved=False. Teacher models ready→playing; pairs predict later rows. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-2; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .
slides.strategy: Guided state trace with faded support

slides.title: A function can change its argument
body: Predict which values the caller sees.
Which function returns a new value?
slides.notes: Call rules.update(state,1,250,collect=False) from a playing interior state: x 308→358, remaining 20000→19750. With mode paused, the same call changes neither value. new_state returns a value; update deliberately mutates its argument and returns None. Its direction, dt_ms and collect parameters receive 1,250,False here. Assigning x=999 to an unrelated local name has no effect on state["x"]. Drawing reads state but must not call update. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-2; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Worked files and changed scaffold are public formative resources. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .
slides.code:
state = rules.new_state()
rules.command(state, "space")
rules.update(state, 1, 250, collect=False)
print(state["x"], state["remaining"])

slides.title: Complete the changed state transitions
body: In faded_practice.py, complete command().
Reset must restore every changed initial value.
Test a paused update for 95000 milliseconds.
slides.notes: Use a COPY of faded_practice.py. Changed initial values are x=40, remaining=15000, active=[True,True,True], score=0 and saved=False. Complete Space transitions and reset using new_state; keep the runner and collision/file code supplied or temporarily out of scope. For movement-only practice, complete only the paused/ready/finished guard and bounded movement/timer part of update with collect=False. Keep stations and persistence for later lessons. Make a fresh state per test. A paused 95000 ms update must leave position and remaining unchanged. For playing x=40, direction1,250 ms at speed160 gives x80 and14750 ms. Do not import the worked solution into the independent rules file. Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-2; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .
slides.strategy: Independent faded task and test record

slides.title: Does a local name explain mutation?
body: command(state, "reset") changes the supplied state.
A: A function can never affect its caller’s data.
B: Changing a shared state slot is caller-visible.
slides.notes: B. Local parameter names refer to objects; deliberately changing shared contents is visible. Rebinding a local parameter to a new object is different. Use an actual reset trace, not an assertion that every function changes globals. If learners choose A, compare one local scalar assignment with state["mode"]="paused". Teaching lab and matching workbook: https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/index.html#y11-2; https://edugenio.github.io/cs-atar-textbook/pygame/workbook.md. Relevant Pygame references: https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/event.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/time.html ; https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/rect.html .

slides.title: Explain a return and a reset
body: Identify parameters and arguments in one call.
Show reset restores a fresh active list.
Explain why paused time stays unchanged.
slides.notes: Use two fresh states: mutate one active flag and show the other still True; after reset, the changed version restores all three flags. Ask for a new unseen action sequence without the reference open. Record expected/actual and support in y11-2 workbook/readiness. Missing evidence means reteach before project issue. No claim of classroom completion is made by this suggested timing. lessons.title: Local names and program structure
lessons.prepare: Python editor and separate caller/function trace columns.

slides.title: Local names and program structure
slides.notes: Success means distinguish local and module-level names, trace simple shadowing and refactor a calculation with explicit inputs and result. Global means module-level in these examples.
body: Unit 1 · Week 5 · Lesson 3
Keep a function’s local work separate from its caller.

slides.title: Retrieval: a reusable result
slides.notes: Parameters appear in definition, arguments in call, return sends a value to caller, print displays output. Retrieve individually then compare before a brief correction. This prepares scope without introducing a new calculation.
body: What are parameters and arguments?
Why return a result that another calculation needs?
What does a call without an explicit return value return?
Compare and correct one explanation.

slides.title: Where names belong
slides.notes: Output 12 then 2. Global quantity starts 2. Local parameter quantity receives 4 and unit_price 3; local result 12 returns and caller cost becomes 12. This does not rebind global quantity. Ask learners to annotate caller and local columns. Same spelling does not imply the same binding.
body: Predict both printed values.
Which quantity belongs to the current call?
slides.code:
quantity = 2
def badge_cost(quantity, unit_price):
    result = quantity * unit_price
    return result
cost = badge_cost(4, 3)
print(cost)
print(quantity)

slides.title: A scope record for one call
slides.notes: Model global quantity 2 and local quantity 4, then learners complete local result 12 and caller cost 12. A fresh call badge_cost(6,5) returns 30 while global quantity stays 2. Parameters and assigned names inside this function are local. Module-level code cannot directly use its local result name.

slides.title: A local assignment
slides.notes: Output 9 then 2. x=9 creates a local binding; global x remains 2. The caller receives 9 through return. A function can read global names, but local assignment does not automatically change a global. Global declarations are outside the core task. Avoid saying globals cannot be read inside functions.
body: Predict before running.
Explain why the two outputs differ.
slides.code:
x = 2
def local_demo():
    x = 9
    return x
print(local_demo())
print(x)

slides.title: Refactoring the badge calculation
slides.notes: Write badge_cost(quantity,unit_price) returning product. Keep prompts and receipt output in caller. Test (0,3)->0, (4,3)->12, (4,5)->20 before interactive input. Explicit parameters make dependencies visible rather than relying on changing global prices. Support: provide a definition skeleton. Stretch: explain why a new price argument changes that call’s result. Peer checks compare behaviour before/after.
body: Move the badge calculation into badge_cost.
Pass quantity and price as arguments.
Keep input prompts and receipt printing in the caller.
Test the calculation first, then the whole program.

slides.title: Does the global value change?
slides.notes: Correct A: module-level x stays 2 in local_demo. B is the returned local value 9. Take responses before discussion. If several choose B, use separate trace columns. Returning 9 differs from assigning a new global x.
body: In local_demo, a local x is set to 9.
The module-level x started at 2.
After the call, module-level x is A: 2     B: 9
Choose alone and justify using scope.

slides.title: Exit ticket: trace scope
slides.notes: With global quantity 2 and badge_cost(3,5), result 15 returns, local quantity 3 and global quantity 2. Caller receives the local calculation through return. Collect individual traces and use errors to plan support for the delivery function.
body: Keep module-level quantity at 2.
Call badge_cost(3, 5) and predict its result.
State the local and module-level quantity values.
How can the caller receive a locally calculated result?

lessons.title: A delivery function with tests
lessons.prepare: Python editor and input/expected/actual log. Assume suitable non-negative numeric order totals.

slides.title: A delivery function with tests
slides.notes: Success means implement a contract, return the correct charge and test below/at/above 50. Formative transfer uses the chapter’s existing delivery rule.
body: Unit 1 · Week 5 · Lesson 4
Test a focused function before adding input and output.

slides.title: Retrieval: the delivery boundary
slides.notes: Totals 49.99,50,50.01 give charges 5,0,0. >=50 includes equality. return supplies a result, print displays output. Retrieve the Week 3 rule individually then compare before designing the function.
body: Recall free delivery for orders of $50 or more.
Predict charges for 49.99, 50 and 50.01.
Which comparison includes exactly 50?
How does return differ from print?

slides.title: A small function contract
slides.notes: Name delivery_charge, one parameter order_total, numeric returned charge. Assume suitable non-negative finite numbers. Invalid text/negative totals are outside this introductory contract. Input and print stay outside the function. Learners underline >=50 and identify caller operations.

slides.title: An early return ends the call
slides.notes: For 50, True returns 0 and ends the call, so return 5 does not run. For 49.99, False leads to return 5. print with 50 displays 0. Learners predict 50.01->0 before running. An explicit else returning 5 is also valid. Focus on returned charge rather than formatted receipt text.
body: Trace totals 50 and 49.99.
Why does a successful call return only one charge?

slides.title: Expectations come from the contract
slides.notes: Before running, calculate 49.99->5,50->0,50.01->0. These distinguish > from >=. Add ordinary 10->5 and 100->0. Support: mark the inclusive boundary on a number line. Stretch: explain why 10 and 100 alone miss equality faults.

slides.title: Your implementation and caller
slides.notes: Re-create from the contract before consulting the model. Make separate calls for boundary totals and 10,100, recording expected/actual. Then add total = float(input("Order total: ")), charge = delivery_charge(total), and print(charge) in caller. Support: header and blank branches. Stretch: store and reuse returned charge in another calculation. No input validation is claimed.
body: Write delivery_charge from the contract.
Test boundary totals and ordinary totals 10 and 100.
Then add input and display in the caller.
Record any correction and rerun the test set.

slides.title: Which test detects the equality fault?
slides.notes: A faulty >50 condition returns 5 at 50 instead of 0. Correct B. 49.99 and 100 still pass. Take simultaneous responses and explain why the repair needs rerunning other tests. If several choose A, compare > and >= at exactly 50 in a trace.
body: A faulty function uses order_total > 50.
Which input reveals the error?
Choose alone, explain and propose the correction.

slides.title: Exit ticket: defend the function
slides.notes: For 50 charge 0; for 25 charge 5. Returning a number supports reuse. Strong evidence includes independent predictions below/at/above 50 with observed results. Collect individual code/test explanations to check calls, parameter mapping, return and scope before Week 6 arrays.
body: State the returned charges for totals 50 and 25.
Explain why input stays outside the function.
Name the test that checks equality at the boundary.
Show how the caller can store and display a result.
